definition: An English umbrella term for the First Peoples of mainland Australia and many of its islands, who comprise hundreds of distinct nations with their own languages, laws and Country. It is not a single identity or culture.

The First Peoples of the Torres Strait islands, between Cape York and Papua New Guinea, with their own languages, cultures and history. They are distinct from Aboriginal peoples, though the two are often named together in Australian policy.

An English word for the continuing creative order in which Ancestral beings shaped Country and law. Many nations use their own terms, such as Jukurrpa in Warlpiri and Tjukurpa in Pitjantjatjara; 'Dreamtime' is a misleading older label.

The land, water, sky and living things to which a nation belongs, understood as a relationship of kinship and responsibility rather than property. Country is not a synonym for wilderness or landscape.

A great serpent of waterholes, rain and law told across many northern nations under different names, such as Ngalyod in Kuninjku country. It is not one pan-Australian figure, and stories and restrictions vary by site.
The sky creator of the Wiradjuri and Kamilaroi peoples of inland New South Wales, who made the land, the first people and the law. Colonial records spell the name in several ways.

The rain-bringing creator ancestors of the Kimberley, painted in rock shelters across Worrorra, Ngarinyin and Wunambal country. They are living sacred figures, repainted by senior men to renew the land, not images of alien visitors.
The Pleiades, understood as Ancestral women whose journey is sung across the Western Desert. Warlpiri and Pitjantjatjara tellings differ, and parts of the story are restricted knowledge.
An English word from Wemba-Wemba or Wergaia country, usually translated as devil or evil spirit. It now covers many different south-eastern water beings, so there is no single pan-Aboriginal bunyip.

A route across Country remembered and performed through song, story, dance and painting, linking places made by Ancestral beings. Songlines are living law and ceremony, not simply maps or tourist trails.
